title: Africa’s industrial window of opportunity: why strategic timing matters
body:
There are moments in global economic history that quietly reshape who produces what, where, and why, and ultimately who captures value.

We are currently living in one of those moments.

The global economy is undergoing a profound reconfiguration: the green transition is accelerating demand for critical minerals and low-carbon technologies

Supply chains are being diversified away from concentrated hubs in Asia in pursuit of resilience, security, and geopolitical risk reduction

Geoeconomic competition is reshaping industrial strategy across major powers and industrial policy is no longer an exception — it is becoming the norm

This global shift creates a rare structural opening for late-industrializing regions.

For Africa, in particular, the implications of these global structural transition are significant.

- The continent sits at the centre of several emerging value chains, from critical minerals for batteries and renewable energy systems, to land, agro-processing potential, and a growing labour force.
- In principle, this is a moment of opportunity. But opportunity is not automatic transformation. Even worse, the same forces that create opportunity can also reproduce dependency and structural retrogression.
- The one million question is thus whether African economies can convert this geopolitical and economic realignment into domestic productive capability.

History offers two important lessons.

- First, global windows of opportunity do not automatically translate into industrial transformation.
- Second, global windows of restructuring do not remain open indefinitely. They quickly harden into new hierarchies.

**Implications:** Africa meaningfully gaining from the ongoing global green transformation will not be determined by its resource endowments. It will be determined by the policy choices and the capabilities the economies within it accummulate. At the same time, these policy choices and capability accumulation are time bound.

This is where strategic timing becomes decisive. Why?

- Countries that move early, with coherent industrial strategy, capable institutions, and coordinated regional markets, will shape the next phase of global production networks.
- Those that do not may find themselves locked into familiar roles, even in a “green” global economy.

**Bottom line:** Without a timely strategic action, Africa risks repeating a familiar pattern: exporting raw materials for the green transition, while importing the technologies, machinery, and high-value components that define it.

The real issue is thus not whether Africa is part of the global shift. It is whether Africa is positioned to shape its terms. That is the challenge of this moment. And it will not wait.
